### Spatial data 1

There are multiple R packages that can be used to load geographic data stored in the *simple features* format. `rnaturalearth` stores data at the global scale: countries and, at finer resolution, their states and provinces. `tigris` stores data from the US Census at a much finer grain of detail: counties, census blocks, zip codes, etc. It is updated yearly.

@. Using the `rnaturalearth` package, download map data for a country of your choosing (not the US or Mexico) in `sf` format. How many simple features are in the data set? What datum was used to record it (see "Geodetic CRS")?

@. Using the `sf` and `ggplot2` packages, make a map of your country[^ne-scale].

[^ne-scale]: If you are unsatisfied with the resolution of your map, you can tinker with the `scale` argument of the `ne_countries()` function.

@. Using the `tigris` package, download a map of California that shows county outlines as of 2024. How many simple features are in the data set? What datum was used to record it?

```{r}
#| eval: false
library(tigris)
ca_counties <- counties(state = "CA", cb = TRUE, year = 2024)
```

@. Make a map of the counties of California two ways: unprojected, in the longitude and latitude the data were recorded in, and projected with the [Albers Equal Area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albers_projection) projection[^albers]. How do the two maps compare?

[^albers]: Each projection has a numeric code (its EPSG code). The Albers Equal Area projection for California is 3310. Pass that code to the `crs` argument of the `st_transform()` function in `sf`.

@. UC Berkeley is host to the Northern California Earthquake Data Center (<https://ncedc.org>). Its records of the earthquakes of magnitude 3 or more in California and nearby, from September 1 to October 16, 2025, are in a csv file. [Download `ca-quakes.csv`](/23-spatial-1/data/ca-quakes.csv) and read it in with the following.

```{r}
#| eval: false
quakes <- read_csv("ca-quakes.csv")
```

Add the locations of these earthquakes to both of your CA maps using `geom_point()`.

@. As you will have noticed, on the Albers map all of the earthquakes land on a single dot in central California. `geom_sf()` drew the counties in Albers coordinates, which are meters east and north of a point near 120° W, 38° N. `geom_point()` took the earthquakes' longitudes and latitudes to be meters too, so it placed every earthquake within about 130 meters of that point. Remake your Albers map the way we fixed the storms in lecture: convert the earthquake data frame to an sf object in WGS 84 (EPSG 4326) with `st_as_sf()`, then transform it to the Albers projection (EPSG 3310) with `st_transform()`[^quakes-sf].

[^quakes-sf]: Hint: since `quakes_albers` is an sf object instead of a tibble, `geom_point()` will no longer work. You can add it in a second `geom_sf()` layer (the first will be for the basemap).

### Spatial II

The following exercises serve as an introduction to the functionality of the `sf` package. Anytime you use a new function, use `?` to learn how it works. Some of these exercises ask you to plot the result. Plots are provided to check your answer.

@. The map of California in lecture was drawn from a shapefile. [Download `CA_State.zip`](/24-spatial-2/data/CA_State.zip), unzip it into the folder you're working in, and read the shapefile in with the following.

```{r}
#| eval: false
library(sf)
ca <- st_read("CA_State/CA_State.shp")
```

Replicate the map of California from lecture, then compute the centroid of the state and add it to the map as a point.

@. *Optional Challenge*: Which county does the centroid of California lie in? Find out computationally, using the `ca_counties` that you downloaded with `tigris` in the Spatial I problems[^ca-crs].

[^ca-crs]: Compare the CRS of `ca_counties` with the CRS of your centroid.

@. Following the approach used in lecture, use `st_linestring` to create two separate line segments called `l1` that stretches from $(0, 0)$ to $(1, 1)$ and `l2` that stretches from $(0, 1)$ to $(1, 0)$. View them using base R `plot()`[^plot-add].

[^plot-add]: Each object will require a separate call to `plot()`. You can add `add = TRUE` to `plot()` so that the contents of the second get added to the first. Note that these plot additions don't carry over from code cell to code cell.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-align: right
library(sf)
l1 <- st_linestring(matrix(c(0, 0,
                                 1, 1),
                                 ncol = 2,
                                 byrow = TRUE))
l2 <- st_linestring(matrix(c(0, 1,
                                 1, 0),
                                 ncol = 2,
                                 byrow = TRUE))
plot(l1)
plot(l2, add = TRUE)
```

@. Form a spatial data frame (an object with classes `sf` and `data.frame`) called `my_lines` with two columns:

1. `id`: an attribute with values `1` and `2`.
1. `geom`: a *simple feature (geometry) column* containing the two lines.

Use the coordinate reference system "OGC:CRS84".

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
my_lines <- st_sf(id = c(1, 2),
                  geom = st_sfc(l1, l2), 
                  crs = 'OGC:CRS84')
```

@. Create a second spatial data frame, this one with a diamond-shaped polygon. The diamond should have corners at $(.5, .8)$, $(.3, .5)$, $(.5, .2)$, and $(.7, .5)$ and use the same crs. It should have an attribute called `price` with the value `100`. Call your spatial data frame `my_diamond` and plot it atop your lines.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-align: right
d1 <- st_polygon(list(matrix(c(.5, .8, .3, .5, .5, .2, .7, .5, .5, .8), ncol = 2, byrow = TRUE)))
plot(l1)
plot(l2, add = TRUE)
plot(d1, add = TRUE)
my_diamond <- st_sf(price = 100,
                    geom = st_sfc(d1),
                    crs = 'OGC:CRS84')
```

@. Calculate the dimension, length, and area of `my_lines`.

@. Calculate the dimension, length, and area of `my_diamond`.

@. Use the `st_split()` function inside the `lwgeom` package to split the diamond into four diamonds using your lines and name the resulting object `split_diamond`. After inspecting the result, run the following line to extract each of the polygons into a separate feature (row) of a spatial data frame.

```{r}
#| eval: false
#| echo: true
split_diamond <- split_diamond |>
    st_collection_extract("POLYGON")
```

Plot the resulting sf collection of 4 features, with each of the split diamonds filled with a color[^plot-col].

[^plot-col]: You can add colors to `plot()` using the `col` argument and call `colors()` at the console to see the color names available in base R. I used `col = c("skyblue", "tomato")` but you're welcome to pick your own colors.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-align: right
library(lwgeom)
split_diamond <- st_split(my_diamond, my_lines)
split_diamond <- st_collection_extract(split_diamond, "POLYGON") |> 
    st_sf()
plot(st_geometry(split_diamond), col = c("skyblue", "tomato"))
```

@. Compute the centroids of the four split diamonds, call them `my_cents`, and add them to your plot. Set their `col` and `pch` as you like.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-align: right
my_cents <- split_diamond |>
  st_centroid()
plot(st_geometry(split_diamond), col = c("skyblue", "tomato"))
plot(my_cents, add = TRUE, pch = 16, col = "white")
```

@. Using what you know about data frame subsetting, remove the bottom-most centroid. Then take the union of the three remaining points, form a convex hull from them, and save the polygon to `my_tri_up`[^set-ops]. Plot `my_tri_up` on top of your split diamond.

[^set-ops]: The functions for these set operations in `sf` are exactly as you'd expect: the name of the operation prepended by `st_`. Note also that the union operation will drop the `sf` class. You'll need to run your object through `st_sf()` to get it back.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-align: right
my_tri_up <- my_cents |>
    slice(-3) |>
    st_union() |>
    st_convex_hull() |>
    st_sf()
plot(st_geometry(split_diamond), col = c("skyblue", "tomato"))
plot(my_tri_up, add = TRUE)
```

@. Repeat the previous exercise, but form an sf object called `my_tri_down` that has the top-most centroid removed.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-align: right
my_tri_down <- my_cents |>
    slice(-1) |>
    st_union() |>
    st_convex_hull() |>
    st_sf()
plot(st_geometry(split_diamond), col = c("skyblue", "tomato"))
plot(my_tri_down, add = TRUE)
```

@. Under the definition of "intersects", which of your split diamonds intersect the `my_tri_up`? Check by doing a spatial join.

### Gerrymandering

Recall the three quantitative approaches to measuring gerrymandering discussed in lecture:

1. Mean - Median Score (Grofman, 1983)
2. Efficiency Gap (Stephanopoulos and McGee, 2015)
3. Ensembles / Extreme Outliers

Use the following election results to practice applying the first two.

| District | D Votes | R Votes | Result  |
|:---------:|:-------:|:-------:|:--------|
| 1 | 62 | 38 | D wins |
| 2 | 55 | 45 | D wins |
| 3 | 44 | 56 | R wins |
| 4 | 47 | 53 | R wins |
| 5 | 46 | 54 | R wins |
| **Total** | **254** | **246** |          |

To work with them in R, create the following data frame.

```{r}
#| label: gerry-votes
#| message: false
library(tidyverse)
votes <- tibble(District = 1:5,
                d_votes = c(62, 55, 44, 47, 46),
                r_votes = c(38, 45, 56, 53, 54),
                result = c(rep("D wins", 2), rep("R wins", 3)))
```

@. Calculate the mean-median score associated with this particular district breakdown of votes.

@. Calculate the efficiency gap (EG) associated with this particular district breakdown of votes[^wasted-fn].

[^wasted-fn]: It may be helpful to write a function that takes a vector of votes across districts for party A and a vector of votes for party B and returns a vector of the number of votes wasted by party A across districts.

### Dashboards

Starting from the contents of `demo-dashboard.qmd` found in the corresponding repo (<https://github.com/berkeley-stat133/demo-dashboard>) create a data dashboard the provides information on the most recent earthquakes to strike New Zealand. The dashboard should include:

1. Your name added as the author.
1. A theme of your choosing[^th].
1. A layout in two columns.
1. The map of New Zealand taking up the full right column.
1. The left of column should two rows, the top of which has value boxes for the number of hours since the last earthquake and the number of earthquakes in the last 24 hours. Select a suitable icon for each[^dash].
1. The bottom row should hold the table of the top n earthquakes.
1. All of the above should be on a page called "Dashboard". Add a second page called "About the data" that displays the following:

> The original author of this dashboard is Charlotte Wickham.
> 
> The data on earthquakes is drawn from the GeoNet API:
> 
> <https://api.geonet.org.nz/>
> 
> All earthquakes below MMI 3.0 have been filtered out.

Since it is quite lengthy, there is no need to copy the code used in your dashboard into this problem set. 

[^th]: Dashboards collect the colors and fonts into themes similar to ggplot2. You can find the list of themes here: <https://quarto.org/docs/dashboards/theming.html>.

[^dash]: Quarto dashboards can use any of the icons in a large collection called Bootstrap. Search for an icon and then use the corresponding name as a string: <https://icons.getbootstrap.com/>.

### R Packages

Select one of the following packages to investigate the structure of. Each one is an example of a small package that does one thing well.

1. `reprex` (<https://github.com/tidyverse/reprex>): makes reproducible examples of code to post to forums for help.
1. `glue` (<https://github.com/tidyverse/glue>): glues strings together.
1. `fs` (<https://github.com/r-lib/fs>): tools for working with your file system.
1. `janitor`(<https://github.com/sfirke/janitor>): simple data cleaning helpers.

@. Who is the first author of the package? Where did you find this information?

@. What is the official one sentence description of the package?

@. How many functions does the package export to the user? Where did you find this information?

@. What is the path to the r script that holds the source of the first exported function?

@. Try running the first examples that show up in the README. Where could you have used the package on any of your previous projects?

@. Using `package.skeleton()`, create a package called `greetr` that holds just one item: the function `hello()`. Sketch the file tree of the package below.

@. Fill in `DESCRIPTION` with information suitable to this simple package (you can pick your own version number and I recommend the MIT license). Write your description file below.
